2.1.title: Algorithms with Selection and Repetition

objectives.text: Describe the behavior of a given segment that uses sequencing, selection, and iteration.

iCan: I can name the three building blocks of an algorithm and point to each one in a segment of code.
I can read a flowchart and say which building block each shape represents.
I can explain why the order of steps changes the result, using an example where swapping two steps changes the output.

lesson_page.intro: The Topic 2.1 lesson page has the building-block identification exercise, the six checks for understanding, and the flowchart game. Everything on that page is auto-graded and lands in your gradebook as students submit.
activities: Run the 2.1 code exercise: given a short segment, label each line as sequencing, selection, or iteration, and check the expected output.
Complete the six checks for understanding. For each flowchart item, trace the arrows with a finger before choosing.
Play the flowchart game for the six rounds it scores. Any round that gets the diamond wrong should be retraced by following the arrows.
Work the FRQ item: describe in prose what a given segment does, without using the words if or while.

2.1.independent: Offline labeling and flowchart drill. Everything below runs on paper.

2.10.title: Implementing String Algorithms

objectives.text: Implement standard algorithms that traverse and build Strings, using the String methods in the AP Java subset.

iCan: I can write a loop that visits every character of a String using length and substring.
I can count the characters or substrings that meet a criterion, and stop the loop at the right index.
I can build a new String from parts, including reversing one, without going out of bounds.

lesson_page.intro: The Topic 2.10 lesson page has the code exercise, the six checks for understanding, and the String traversal game. Everything on that page is auto-graded and lands in your gradebook as students submit.
activities: Run the 2.10 code exercise: count how many times a given letter appears in a word, and confirm the answer for two different words.
Break it on purpose: change the loop condition to i <= s.length(), run it, and read the exception name and the index it reports.
Complete the six checks for understanding. For each substring item, write the length of the result as the second argument minus the first.
Play the String traversal game for the six rounds it scores.

2.10.independent: Offline String drill. Everything below runs on paper.

2.11.title: Nested Iteration

objectives.text: Determine the result or side effect of nested iteration statements, including the total number of executions.

iCan: I can trace a nested loop and say how many times the inner body runs in total.
I can explain why the inner loop completes fully on every single pass of the outer loop.
I can compute the total executions when the inner bound depends on the outer control variable.

lesson_page.intro: The Topic 2.11 lesson page has the code exercise, the six checks for understanding, and the nested loop game. Everything on that page is auto-graded and lands in your gradebook as students submit.
activities: Run the 2.11 code exercise: print a rectangle of characters with a nested loop, then change one bound and confirm the count changes as predicted.
Break it on purpose: move the inner loop's initialization above the outer loop, run it, and say how many times the inner body runs in total.
Complete the six checks for understanding. For each item, write the outer count times the inner count, or the table, before choosing.
Play the nested loop game for the six rounds it scores.

2.11.independent: Offline nesting drill. Everything below runs on paper.

2.12.title: Informal Run-Time Analysis

objectives.text: Compute statement execution counts for code segments containing iteration, and compare the efficiency of algorithms informally.

iCan: I can count exactly how many times a given statement executes in a segment with one or more loops.
I can say how the execution count grows when the input size doubles, for a single loop and for a nested pair.
I can compare two algorithms that produce the same result and say which does less work, with a count rather than an opinion.

lesson_page.intro: The Topic 2.12 lesson page has the code exercise, the six checks for understanding, and the counting game. Everything on that page is auto-graded and lands in your gradebook as students submit.
activities: Run the 2.12 code exercise: add a counter that increments on every pass of a nested loop, print it, and check it against the count you predicted.
Break it on purpose: move the inner loop so the two loops become sequential rather than nested, run it again, and compare the two counters.
Complete the six checks for understanding. For each item, write the count beside every line before choosing an answer.
Play the counting game for the six rounds it scores.

2.12.independent: Offline counting drill. Everything below runs on paper.

2.2.title: Boolean Expressions

objectives.text: Evaluate Boolean expressions that use relational operators.

iCan: I can evaluate any of the six relational operators on two numbers and give the boolean result.
I can explain why == compares references rather than contents when both operands are objects.
I can store a relational result in a boolean variable and use that variable directly as a condition.

lesson_page.intro: The Topic 2.2 lesson page has the code exercise, the six checks for understanding, and the operator game. Everything on that page is auto-graded and lands in your gradebook as students submit.
activities: Run the 2.2 code exercise: print the result of all six relational operators on a pair of values you choose, and predict each result before running.
Break it on purpose: change one == to a single =, run it, and read the compiler message.
Complete the six checks for understanding. For any item using <= or >=, say the operator before answering.
Play the operator game for the six rounds it scores.

2.2.independent: Offline evaluation drill and bug hunt. Everything below runs on paper.

2.3.title: if Statements

objectives.text: Determine the result of conditional statements, including one-way and two-way selection.

iCan: I can trace an if statement and say whether the body runs, for any value of the condition.
I can explain the difference between two separate if statements and one if-else, and show an input where they behave differently.
I can find the four classic if-statement bugs in code: missing braces, a stray semicolon, = instead of ==, and a dangling else.

lesson_page.intro: The Topic 2.3 lesson page has the code exercise, the six checks for understanding, and the trace game. Everything on that page is auto-graded and lands in your gradebook as students submit.
activities: Run the 2.3 code exercise: write an if statement that prints 'Pass' only when a score of 60 or more is stored in the variable, and confirm the expected output for both a passing and a failing value.
Break it on purpose: put a semicolon straight after the condition, run it again, and read what changed about the output.
Complete the six checks for understanding. For every item that hinges on braces, underline the statement the if actually controls before choosing an answer.
Play the trace game for the six rounds it scores. Students who finish early trace a partner's wrong answer back to the line that caused it.

2.3.independent: Offline bug hunt and trace drill. Everything below runs on paper.

2.4.title: Nested if Statements

objectives.text: Determine the result of nested conditional statements and multiway selection.

iCan: I can trace a nested if and name which conditions were evaluated and which were skipped entirely.
I can write an if-else-if chain that assigns exactly one category to every possible input.
I can explain why reordering the branches of an if-else-if chain can change the result even when every condition is correct.

lesson_page.intro: The Topic 2.4 lesson page has the code exercise, the six checks for understanding, and the nested-if trace game. Everything on that page is auto-graded and lands in your gradebook as students submit.
activities: Run the 2.4 code exercise: build the two-gate ride check as a nested if and confirm the output for all four combinations of pass and fail.
Break it on purpose: remove the braces from the outer if and add a statement after the inner block, then run it and explain which if now owns that statement.
Complete the six checks for understanding. For each item, write down how many conditions were evaluated before choosing an answer.
Play the nested-if trace game for the six rounds it scores.

2.4.independent: Offline chain analysis. Everything below runs on paper.

2.5.title: Compound Boolean Expressions

objectives.text: Evaluate compound Boolean expressions that use logical operators, including short-circuit evaluation.

iCan: I can evaluate an expression using &&, ||, and ! and give the boolean result for any combination of operands.
I can say which operand of a compound expression is not evaluated, and why, in a short-circuit case.
I can apply the precedence order ! then && then || to an expression with no parentheses.

lesson_page.intro: The Topic 2.5 lesson page has the code exercise, the six checks for understanding, and the truth-table game. Everything on that page is auto-graded and lands in your gradebook as students submit.
activities: Run the 2.5 code exercise: write a range check with && and confirm it accepts values inside the range and rejects values on both sides of it.
Break it on purpose: swap the two operands of a && whose left side is a guard, feed it the value the guard was protecting against, and read what happens.
Complete the six checks for understanding. For each item, write the number of operands actually evaluated before choosing an answer.
Play the truth-table game for the six rounds it scores.

2.5.independent: Offline evaluation and precedence drill. Everything below runs on paper.

2.6.title: Comparing Boolean Expressions

objectives.text: Determine whether two Boolean expressions are equivalent, including by applying De Morgan's law.
Compare object references using == and equals.

iCan: I can build a truth table for two expressions and use it to decide whether they are equivalent.
I can apply De Morgan's law to rewrite a negated compound condition without the outer ! operator.
I can say what == compares on object references and when equals gives a different answer.

lesson_page.intro: The Topic 2.6 lesson page has the code exercise, the six checks for understanding, and the equivalence game. Everything on that page is auto-graded and lands in your gradebook as students submit.
activities: Run the 2.6 code exercise: print an expression and its De Morgan rewrite for all four combinations of two booleans and confirm the outputs match line for line.
Break it on purpose: drop the operator flip so the rewrite reads !a && !b, run it again, and name the combination where the outputs diverge.
Complete the six checks for understanding. For any equivalence item, sketch the four-row table in the margin before answering.
Play the equivalence game for the six rounds it scores.

2.6.independent: Offline equivalence and reference drill. Everything below runs on paper.

2.7.title: while Loops

objectives.text: Determine the result or side effect of iteration statements, including loops that execute zero times and loops that do not terminate.
Represent iterative processes using a while loop.

iCan: I can trace a while loop and state how many times the body executes, including when the answer is zero.
I can name the three parts every loop needs and point to each one in a segment.
I can find the reason a loop never terminates and fix it by changing exactly one line.

lesson_page.intro: The Topic 2.7 lesson page has the code exercise, the six checks for understanding, and the loop trace game. Everything on that page is auto-graded and lands in your gradebook as students submit.
activities: Run the 2.7 code exercise: write a while loop that sums the whole numbers from 1 to a given limit, and confirm the total for two different limits.
Break it on purpose: set the starting value past the limit, run it, and confirm the body executes zero times and the total stays at its initial value.
Complete the six checks for understanding. For each item, write the number of passes in the margin before choosing an answer.
Play the loop trace game for the six rounds it scores.

2.7.independent: Offline trace and bug hunt. Everything below runs on paper.

2.8.title: for Loops

objectives.text: Represent iterative processes using a for loop, including converting between equivalent for and while loops.

iCan: I can name the three parts of a for loop header and say exactly when each one executes.
I can convert any for loop into an equivalent while loop and back again.
I can state how many times a for loop body runs from its header alone, without tracing every pass.

lesson_page.intro: The Topic 2.8 lesson page has the code exercise, the six checks for understanding, and the loop conversion game. Everything on that page is auto-graded and lands in your gradebook as students submit.
activities: Run the 2.8 code exercise: write a for loop that prints the first n whole numbers, and confirm the count for two different values of n.
Break it on purpose: change the condition from < to <=, run it again, and name the extra value that appears.
Complete the six checks for understanding. For each item, write the pass count from the header before tracing anything.
Play the loop conversion game for the six rounds it scores.

2.8.independent: Offline conversion and counting drill. Everything below runs on paper.

2.9.title: Implementing Selection and Iteration Algorithms

objectives.text: Implement standard algorithms that use selection and iteration, including divisibility, digit extraction, counting, and finding minimum and maximum values.

iCan: I can use the modulus operator to test divisibility and to pull individual digits out of a number.
I can write the accumulator pattern for a sum, a count, and an average, and say what each variable starts at.
I can write a minimum or maximum loop that is correct even when every value is negative.

lesson_page.intro: The Topic 2.9 lesson page has the code exercise, the six checks for understanding, and the algorithm game. Everything on that page is auto-graded and lands in your gradebook as students submit.
activities: Run the 2.9 code exercise: write the digit-sum loop and confirm it for a three-digit and a one-digit input.
Break it on purpose: swap the two lines so the division happens before the remainder, run it, and say which digit gets lost.
Complete the six checks for understanding. For each divisibility item, write the modulus expression in the margin before choosing.
Play the algorithm game for the six rounds it scores.

3.1.title: Abstraction and Program Design

objectives.text: Use data abstraction to represent what an object knows, choosing between an attribute each object owns and one the whole class shares.
Use procedural abstraction to represent what an object does, naming a process and decomposing it into methods each responsible for one job.

iCan: I can read a specification and decide which nouns become attributes and which verbs become behaviors.
I can decide whether an attribute belongs to each object or to the whole class, and justify the choice.
I can replace a repeated condition with a named helper method and explain what the name buys the reader.

lesson_page.intro: The Topic 3.1 lesson page has the six checks for understanding, the design decision rounds, and the editor problems.
activities: Work the six checks for understanding. Each one is a design decision, not a syntax question.
Editor problems 1 and 2 are trace problems: read the class and the client code and predict the printed values before running anything.
Editor problem 3 asks for one counter for the whole class. Decide which of the two variables gets static before typing.
Editor problem 5 is the every-ticket-says-1 bug. Find it by asking how many copies of the counter exist.
Editor problem 7 gives a finished class missing its three attributes. Place each one at the right level and say why.

3.1.independent: Design review on paper. Nothing below needs a computer.

3.2.title: Impact of Program Design

objectives.text: State the preconditions a method assumes and the postconditions it guarantees, and explain that a precondition is documented rather than enforced.
Describe how a design decision inside a class affects the people the program is used on, including who is excluded by the values a class can hold.

iCan: I can write the precondition and postcondition for a method and say which one the caller is responsible for.
I can explain why a documented precondition does not stop a caller from breaking it, and what the method does when they do.
I can name a design decision in a small class that would exclude or misrepresent a real person, and propose a change.

lesson_page.intro: The Topic 3.2 lesson page has the checks and practice questions.
activities: Work the checks for understanding. Each asks you to sort a sentence into precondition or postcondition.
Two items give a method with a broken precondition and ask what the object's state is afterwards. Trace it; do not guess that an error occurs.
One item asks you to rewrite a documented precondition as a defensive check and state the new postcondition.
Finish the mastery set. Predict your answer before reading the options.

3.2.independent: On paper. Nothing below needs a computer.

3.3.title: Anatomy of a Class

objectives.text: Identify the parts of a class declaration in order, and state the effect of declaring each part public or private.
Explain that private draws its wall around the class rather than around each object, and that every object of the class carries its own copy of each instance variable.

iCan: I can name the four parts of a class in the order they are written and point to each one in a listing.
I can say what public and private each mean, and predict which lines of client code will fail to compile.
I can explain why one object of a class may reach another object's private variable.

lesson_page.intro: The Topic 3.3 lesson page has the checks, the editor problems, and the encapsulation rounds.
activities: Work the six checks for understanding. Several ask which client lines compile, so read the access modifier before the variable name.
The first editor problem is a trace over a class with a private helper. Predict the printed value before running it.
One editor problem asks you to write a method comparing two objects of the same class. Reach the other object's field directly rather than adding an accessor.
One editor problem gives a class whose setter accepts anything. Replace it with a mutator that enforces one rule and reports whether it acted.
Finish the multiple choice set, predicting each answer before reading the options.

3.3.independent: Offline reading and repair. Everything below runs on paper.

3.4.title: Constructors

objectives.text: Write a constructor that puts every attribute into a valid starting state, and identify a constructor by its name and its absent return type.
Overload constructors so one class offers several ways to be created, and state the default value Java gives an attribute a constructor does not set.

iCan: I can write a constructor that leaves no attribute meaningless, and say why that is the constructor's job rather than a caller's.
I can write two constructors for one class and say which one a given new expression calls.
I can state the default value of an int, a double, a boolean, and an object reference that a constructor never assigns.

lesson_page.intro: The Topic 3.4 lesson page has the checks and editor problems.
activities: Work the six checks for understanding. Several give a class and ask which new expressions compile.
The first editor problems are traces over classes with two or three constructors. Decide which constructor runs before predicting any value.
One editor problem gives a class whose constructor leaves one attribute unset. Say what that attribute's value is, then set it deliberately.
One editor problem has a class that will not compile because two constructors share a signature. Fix it without deleting either behavior.

objectives.text: Write void and return methods with correct headers, and ensure every path through a non-void method returns a value.

iCan: I can write a method header and say from it alone what the method gives back and what it needs.
I can find the path through a non-void method that returns nothing and name the compile error it causes.

objectives.text: Declare and create an array using new with a size or using an initializer list, and state the default value of its elements.
Read and update an element by index, use length, and identify the indices that throw ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

iCan: I can create an array two different ways and say when each one is the right choice.
I can name the first and last valid index of an array of any size, and say what length reports.
I can predict whether a given index throws, and name the exception it throws.

lesson_page.intro: The Topic 4.3 lesson page has the checks and editor problems.
activities: Work the checks for understanding. Several give an array and an index and ask whether it throws.
The creation items ask which of two forms to use. Decide whether the values are known yet before choosing.
One item asks for the value at an index that was never assigned. Give the type's default rather than saying undefined.
One item creates an array of objects and calls a method on an element. Say which exception it throws and why it is not out of bounds.
Finish the mastery set, predicting each answer before reading the options.

4.3.independent: Offline. Everything below runs on paper.

4.4.title: Traversing Arrays

objectives.text: Traverse an array with a standard for loop, including in reverse and over part of the array, and update elements during the traversal.
Traverse an array with an enhanced for loop, and state what the enhanced form cannot do.

iCan: I can write the standard traversal from memory and say what each of the three parts of the header does.
I can choose between a standard for loop and an enhanced for loop by asking whether I need the index or need to write.
I can find an off-by-one error by counting the passes rather than reading the code.

lesson_page.intro: The Topic 4.4 lesson page has the checks and editor problems.
activities: Work the checks for understanding. For each loop, count the passes before deciding anything else.
Several items ask whether a loop throws, skips an element, or is correct. Check the start and the bound separately.
One item asks you to write a partial traversal. Decide which of the three header parts to change.
One item tries to modify elements with an enhanced for loop. Say what actually happens to the array.
Finish the mastery set, predicting each answer before reading the options.

4.4.independent: Offline. Everything below runs on paper.

4.5.title: Algorithms with Arrays

objectives.text: Implement the standard array algorithms: minimum and maximum, sum and average, linear search, and frequency count.
Apply the same algorithms to an array of objects by reading one attribute out of each element.

iCan: I can write a maximum loop and say why it is initialized from element 0 rather than from 0.
I can write both forms of linear search, the one returning a boolean and the one returning an index.
I can adapt any of the standard algorithms to an array of objects by changing only the body.

lesson_page.intro: The Topic 4.5 lesson page has the checks and editor problems.
activities: Work the checks for understanding. Each names an algorithm and asks for its starting value.
Two items initialize an extreme to 0. Find an input that exposes the bug rather than saying it is wrong.
One item asks for the first occurrence and one for the last. Decide whether the loop returns or assigns.
One item computes an average with integer division. Give the printed value, then the fix.
One item applies an algorithm to an array of objects. Change only the body.
Finish the mastery set, predicting each answer before reading the options.

4.8.title: ArrayList Methods

objectives.text: Use the AP reference sheet ArrayList methods: add in both forms, remove, get, set, and size.
Predict how add at an index and remove shift the elements after them, and what each returns.

iCan: I can name every ArrayList method on the reference sheet and say what each one returns.
I can predict the list's contents after a sequence of adds and removes, including the shifting.
I can say which methods change the size and which only change a value.

lesson_page.intro: The Topic 4.8 lesson page has the checks and practice items.
activities: Work the checks for understanding. For each call, write the list's contents and its size afterwards.
Two items use set where add was meant, or the reverse. Say what the size reveals.
One item asks what each method returns. Use the reference sheet rather than guessing.
One item adds at an index equal to size. Decide whether it throws before choosing.
Finish the mastery set, predicting each answer before reading the options.

4.9.title: Traversing ArrayLists

objectives.text: Traverse an ArrayList with a standard for loop and with an enhanced for loop, and choose between them.
Remove elements during a traversal correctly, and explain why the obvious forward loop skips elements.

iCan: I can write both traversals for a list and say what size() does in each.
I can explain why removing inside a forward loop skips the element after every removal.
I can write the two correct removal traversals and say what each one costs.

lesson_page.intro: The Topic 4.9 lesson page has the checks and practice items.
activities: Work the checks for understanding. For each removal loop, decide correct, skips, or throws.
Two items give data with adjacent matches and data without. Say why the same loop passes one and fails the other.
One item asks you to convert a skipping loop into a correct one, two different ways.
One item calls set inside an enhanced for. Decide whether it throws before choosing.
Finish the mastery set, predicting each answer before reading the options.
